name: Modal Interrogative Request
pattern: polar interrogative with can/could/will/would and second-person subject

entry.name: Modal Interrogative Request
entry.pattern: polar interrogative with can/could/will/would and second-person subject

1.definition: Uses interrogative form to request the addressee’s action.

projection.target: Lowering the shade can satisfy the utterance. In a capacity-testing context the same form can instead invite an answer about ability.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Questions that are really requests
curious.summary: A yes-or-no question with can, could, will or would and you can be a way to ask someone to do something.
curious.body: Could you lower the shade? has the form of a question, but the speaker wants the shade lowered. The listener can satisfy it by doing that, rather than by answering yes or no. The pattern is a yes-or-no question with can, could, will or would and you as the subject. The same words can also be a real question. If the setting is a test of what someone is able to do, Could you lower the shade? can invite an answer about ability instead.
curious.try: Next time you ask someone for help with Can you ... or Could you ..., notice whether they answer in words or just do it.

teacher.summary: Useful for teaching requests: the interrogative form with a modal and you asks for action.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a polar interrogative with can, could, will or would and a second-person subject, used to request the addressee's action. The same form can also be a literal question; the use differs. Could you lower the shade? can be satisfied by lowering the shade. In a capacity-testing context the same form can invite an answer about ability. Teachers can contrast it with the imperative, which this dictionary lists as a related construction. This dictionary classes the pattern as pragmatic: it concerns how the form is used.
teacher.terms: Indirect speech act or indirect request are textbook names for this kind of use.

contrasts.note: A request; lowering the shade satisfies it.

watch_for: A learner might answer Could you lower the shade? with only yes, taking it as a question about ability.
teacher.activity: Students write three requests with can, could or would and you for a classroom situation (a closed window, a lost pen). In pairs, one reads the request and the other responds with an action, not words. Discuss when a spoken answer would be expected instead.

child.hook: When someone asks "Can you pass the salt?", do they want just a yes?
child.explain: Some questions are really ways of asking for something. Could you lower the shade? asks you to lower it. You can answer by doing it.
child.play: Ask a friend to do something with Could you or Will you. They answer by doing it, not by speaking. Then swap.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer mentions willingness questions (the entry supports only the capacity-testing ability reading). Also fixed (unflagged): removed 'polite' from curious.summary and teacher.summary and cut the watch_for about a future reading, since the entry supports neither.
